# Leveraging Predictions of Task-Related Latents for Interactive Visual Navigation

Jiwei Shen , Liang Yuan , Member, IEEE, Yue Lu , Senior Member, IEEE, and Shujing Lyu

**Abstract— Interactive visual navigation (IVN) involves tasks where embodied agents learn to interact with the objects in the environment to reach the goals. Current approaches exploit visual features to train a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation control policy network. However, RL-based methods continue to struggle at the IVN tasks as they are inefficient in learning a good representation of the unknown environment in partially observable settings. In this work, we introduce predictions of task-related latents (PTRLs), a flexible self-supervised RL framework for IVN tasks. PTRL learns the latent structured information about environment dynamics and leverages multistep representations of the sequential observations. Specifically, PTRL trains its representation by explicitly predicting the next pose of the agent conditioned on the actions. Moreover, an attention and memory module is employed to associate the learned representation to each action and exploit spatiotemporal dependencies. Furthermore, a state value boost module is introduced to adapt the model to previously unseen environments by leveraging input perturbations and regularizing the value function. Sample efficiency in the training of RL networks is enhanced by modular training and hierarchical decomposition. Extensive evaluations have proved the superiority of the proposed method in increasing the accuracy and generalization capacity.**

**Index Terms— Embodied artificial intelligence (AI), interactive visual navigation (IVN), reinforcement learning (RL), representation learning, self-attention.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

NTERACTIVE visual navigation (IVN) stands to benefit I many applications where an agent (e.g., a home robot) takes over the jobs of human beings in a cluttered room, such as patrolling, transportation, and emergency aid. The agent would need to navigate in complex environments from visual perception to complete the services [1]. While classic navigation for autonomous robots is often concerned as a primarily geometric problem for reaching goals with collision avoidance, robots deployed in unstructured real world often present challenges such as pushing objects aside to create a traversable path [2]. As shown in Fig. 1, in order to succeed in the IVN tasks, physical interaction with the objects in the environment should be not only permitted but also encouraged.

The red arrows indicate the direction toward the goal.

A robust strategy with fail-safe guarantees and accuracy for an onboard efficient navigation system is crucial to modern autonomous agents. The agent has to react and execute a driving maneuver using the sensor input. However, the deployment of automated navigation systems faces varied perceptual and interactive complexities of dynamic situations [3]. Mapping from the perception of the high-dimensional nature to the control action remains a significant challenge in the IVN tasks. With the recent advances in deep representations, there has been a significant development in the vision communities [4]. Researchers argue that visual techniques can improve fore active perception in IVN tasks, and there is a stage of development prior to the advent of mature ecosystems for interactive and embodied visual artificial intelligence (AI). The focus of IVN tasks is to enable the agent to learn to reach its goal through interaction with its environment, using its egocentric observations [5]. Consequently, the IVN tasks pose significant challenges for both reinforcement learning (RL) and representation learning.

Representation learning is particularly important in IVN tasks, where learning a representation of the unseen scenarios is crucial to solve the tasks. Navigation with an understanding of these representations in unseen scenarios is an exemplary feat of the human mind. In the IVN tasks, representation learning is an essential component because the agent is in a partially observable environment [6]. The methods in prior work mostly learn the state representation indirectly through the performance prioritization in RL tasks [7]. The end-to-end approaches simultaneously train a visual encoder network alongside a navigation control policy network. Abstract features can be learned by the state representation learning model to characterize the egocentric observation [8]. However, largecapacity encoders may overfit the training scenarios, while smaller encoders may result in limited performance with impoverished representations. Meanwhile, recent research in RL has helped the agents complete the navigation tasks by interacting with the environment [9]. While progress in RL has been ongoing, the performance of the IVN tasks still can significantly degenerate in a poorly fitting scenario. This is because the typically sparse reward signal and limited environment interaction render it ineffective for learning more general concepts applicable in previously unseen scenarios [10]. Navigation models struggle with generalizing to pre-viously unseen scenarios [11]. Thus, training embodied AI models that are interactive and can generalize to previously unseen scenarios remains a significant challenge.

In this work, we introduce predictions of task-related latents (PTRLs), a new framework for IVN tasks. The contribution mainly focuses on how to learn the task-related latents by modular training, including a pose estimation module, an attention and memory module, and a state value boost module. More specifically, the following conditions hold.

1) The pose estimation module estimates the next pose of the agent conditioned on actions that the agent may take. As an alternative to the limited supervision across the training procedure, we introduce supervised pose estimation tasks to improve the performance of representation encodes. The pose estimation module utilizes a navigation-related auxiliary loss to learn representations of the environment. Hence, the learned representations encode important latent information about the deployed environment. The fully supervised fashion of the prediction tasks can help the model understand the environment better. Besides, the visual encoder is also used by the downstream RL navigation control policy network. The visual encoder receives gradients from the pose estimation tasks and the navigation policy. Therefore, additional supervision makes the RL training process more stable by avoiding training downstream navigation control policy network from image pixels directly.

2) Furthermore, PTRL maintains past observations and actions in detailed memories. The attention and memory module is introduced to implicitly associate the learned representation to each action and exploit spatiotemporal dependencies over the task execution.

3) The state value boost module is utilized to perturb the observations and induce an appropriate representation for the policy network to reduce overfitting in training scenarios. The proposed state value boost module led to the winning entry of the interactive navigation track in the CVPR-2021 iGibson Challenge.<sup>1</sup> Extensive experiments and evaluations in high-fidelity simulators demonstrate that the proposed PTRL framework yields excellent performance in heterogeneous scenarios.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. The related work is given in Section II. The details of the proposed framework are elaborated in Section III. Extensive simulation results and discussions are presented in Section IV followed by our conclusion in Section V.

## II. RELATED WORK

In this section, related works are summarized in four major aspects: representation learning for visual navigation, memory for visual navigation, data augmentation for visual navigation, and embodied simulators.

## A. Representation Learning for Visual Navigation

A promising approach to learn an optimal control policy from practice is deep RL, which relies on trial and error learning by interacting with the environment [12]. Deep RL algorithms combine classic RL with deep neural networks to process decision-making from the state representations. The control policy is optimized by maximizing the accumulated rewards by learning from a sequence of control actions globally, rather than the optimal instantaneous action taken locally. However, the training of deep RL is still unstable because it suffers from the demand of the data amount to converge a large network with a set of parameters [13]. Powered by the recent progress in visual scene understanding, the problem of visual navigation has been extensively explored [14]. In order to travel to a designated point [11], [15] or search for a target object [14], [16] in a previously unseen environment, autonomous agents need to reason about egocentric vision intelligently to select the proper sequence of actions. In addition, the vision-and-language navigation (VLN) task, which entails learning to navigate based on natural language instructions, also relies on visual perception for navigation [17]. However, the IVN task poses even greater challenges due to the absence of language instructions and the requirement to navigate through unstructured environments with interactive objects. Moreover, extra texture information of the scenarios and the light variation put a hardbound on representation learning.

With the development of deep RL, methods based on prior task-specific information and methods based on auxiliary tasks are two major paradigms for representation learning. On the one hand, prior knowledge and task-related information can be utilized to improve representation learning. On the other hand, models with auxiliary tasks learn representations with good sample efficiency. For example, compact representations can be learned by reconstructing the images [18], identifying distinct objects [19], [20], detecting concepts of navigation events [21], or recovering the state transfer [22] via generative adversarial networks [23] or autoencoders [24]. Mirowski et al. [25] improved the RL performance in navigation with an auxiliary loop closure classification task and a depth prediction task. Zhao et al. [26] utilized visual odometry and Zeng et al. [27] attempted to predict the external environment in the navigation tasks. Yadav et al. [28] offline pretrained the visual d l i ili l ifi ti t k enco er, emp oy ng an aux ary scene c ass ca on as on an

IID-sampled image dataset. Inspired by prior works, we train the agent with a navigation-related task that predicts the next pose of the agent. Therefore, the performance of policy learning algorithms can be improved with robust representation learning in a fully supervised setting.

## B. Memory for Visual Navigation

To generate good navigation performance in a large unexplored scenario, agents need to perceive the episodic memory and accumulate knowledge of the environment [29]. Recently, Chaplot et al. [30] predicted a top-down map of the environment to plan a path over the tasks’ execution. The received observations are encoded by the neural networks and the memories are saved in the global geometric map, which is conducted simultaneously in navigation. Their work was later improved by using differentiable geometric projections and adding extra channels to encode semantic categories [14]. However, these map-based memory approaches focus only on stationary scenarios, and it is hard to construct a global map for a dynamic environment. Applying recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is a popular choice for endowing an agent’s policy with memory [31]. The input observation and the state vector are stored as scene memory to aggregate the visual and geometric information at every timestep. For instance, Oh et al. [32] proposed to use a memory-based controller to generalize to unseen environments. In this work, we similarly utilize RNN to merge all past observations into the state vector. In addition, we use self-attention mechanisms to exploit spatiotemporal dependencies from the aggregated observations.

## C. Data Augmentation for Visual Navigation

With the recent advances in data augmentation technologies, the performance of supervised computer vision tasks has been significantly improved by injecting the priors of invariance to image augmentations [33], [34], [35]. The label efficiency of downstream vision tasks in unsupervised and semisupervised learning can also be improved with data augmentations [36], [37], [38], [39]. Inspired by the success in computer vision, image augmentation technologies have been investigated in image-based RL and play important roles in achieving the state-of-the-art performance [40]. Yarats et al. [41] added a convolutional encoder and random shifts in the model-free actor–critic framework. Laskin et al. [42] utilized image augmentations to learn contrastive representations jointly with RL. Applying image augmentations is now an essential component of a number of recent RL algorithms [43], [44], [45]. However, image augmentations have been relatively less investigated in the context of visual navigation. In this work, the key idea is to utilize image augmentations and regularize the value function to induce the effect of overfitting to the data distribution in some particular scenarios.

## D. Embodied Simulators

It is valuable to deploy agents directly in physical environments and train models while exposing them to all kinds of situations in the real world. However, current state-of-the-art learning-based algorithms in the embodied AI domain are data and time inefficient [58]. The costs and difficulty of deployment involved in experiments are principal hindrances to progress in IVN. The agents can unwittingly injure the experimental environments and themselves during the training procedure. Moreover, it is not easily reproducible to replicate experiments for researchers. Recently, these difficulties and risks have been alleviated by a host of synthetic environments using physics simulation engines [59], [60], which are introduced to facilitate research for embodied AI. Embodied simulators are designed to simulate a realistic environment and provide an interface for an agent. Equipped with various sensors such as image and position sensors, the agent can interact with this environment. Table I provides a comparative analysis of the existing simulators. Embodied datasets consist of 3-D assets, including textures and meshes, utilized for rendering purposes, accompanied by additional configuration data. These data include object location, object category, and camera pose, which play a crucial role in executing high-level tasks. With the support of a multitude of perceptual simulated environments, object–robot dynamics can be simulated with high precision in handcrafted models, and manipulation strategies can be studied in a safe manner. Interactive environments simulated by embodied simulators, such as AI2-THOR [46], iGibson [56], and RoboTHOR [57], facilitate the interaction with objects in the deployed environment, which is a crucial skill required for real-world robots to accomplish complex tasks.

## III. MODELS

In this section, the IVN tasks are formulated first. Then, the overview of the proposed framework is described, followed by the details of the pose estimation module, the attention and memory module, and the state value boost module.

## A. Problems Formulation

To overcome the challenge raised by the IVN tasks, an RL-based framework is utilized. This kind of decision-making process fits in the framework of the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) that characterizes a process in which an agent takes action generated by a control policy transits to a new state with the observation of the current state and obtains some rewards. The POMDP of the IVN tasks can be defined by a tuple $( \mathcal { S } , \mathcal { A } , \mathcal { O } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { R } )$ . S denotes the state space, and the initial state can be denoted by $s _ { 0 } ,$ where the agent starts to explore the environment. A denotes the predefined action space and consists of all the possible actions that the agent can take. The discrete action executed by the agent at timestep t can be denoted by $a _ { t } \in \mathcal { A } . \mathcal { O }$ denotes the observation space, which is the union of multimodel sensory input, including egocentric RGBD images obtained from the RGBD sensor mounted on the agent and a GPS’s observation given by the environment. $\mathcal { P } ( s _ { t + 1 } \mid s _ { t } , a _ { t } )$ denotes the state-action transition probability. R is the task-related reward function denoted by $\mathcal { R } ( s , a )$

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Schematic of the proposed PTRL framework and the training pipeline. The other task-related embeddings have been omitted for clarity.

The current state of the environment $s _ { t }$ consists of the real-time locations of the agent and the interactive objects. $s _ { t }$ is not available to the agent but is partially observed. The main challenge of RL to solve POMDP is how to train a control policy $\pi ( a | s )$ , which maps the partially observed state to an optimal action for the agent to complete the task. An optimal policy can maximize the expected return, which equals the cumulative reward, defined as: $\mathbb { E } _ { \tau } [ \textstyle \sum _ { t } R ( s _ { t } , a _ { t } ) ]$ where $\tau = ( s _ { t } , a _ { t } ) _ { t = 1 } ^ { H }$ denotes the trajectory of the agent and H denotes the time horizon unrolled by the control policy.

## B. Model Overview

The schematic of the proposed PTRL framework is shown in Fig. 2. The entire model is updated by an RL-based framework via RL loss. A visual encoder receives the RGBD images from the environment and outputs the visual representations. The pose estimation module utilizes the learned representation and task-related embeddings to predict the next pose of the agent at timestep t+1 after applying each action $a _ { t } \in { \mathcal { A } } .$ The ground truth of the agent’s next pose is given by the environment. We optimize the pose estimation module as well as the visual encoder via pose estimation (PE loss) as a regression problem. Moreover, the self-attention layer summarizes the hidden features of previous steps and outputs the action-conditioned state representations to the policy network of the RL module. As shown in Fig. 3, the main components of the attention and memory module are the self-attention layer and the gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based policy network. The self-attention layer handles the spatial embeddings and the GRU-based policy network reason through the temporal information. Then, the agent executes action $a _ { t }$ generated by the policy network to the environment and obtains reward $r _ { t } .$ In addition, the blue arrows in Fig. 2 indicate that the state value boost module generates samples via augmented RGBD images and reuses the visual encoder and policy network to obtain the predicted values of the state. As shown in Fig. 3, lower variance is utilized to regularize the value function of the policy network by averaging the predicted values of the image augmentations in the same state.

The PTRL framework is proposed to investigate the IVN tasks from the following aspects: 1) the pose estimation module can be exploited to obtain robust representations of the environment to enhance the downstream RL; 2) the attention and memory module can associate the learned representation to each action and exploit spatiotemporal dependencies; and 3) the state value boost module can leverage input perturbations and regularizing the value function of RL.

## C. Pose Estimation Module

As shown in Fig. 3, the pose estimation module receives four main components as inputs: the visual features v extracted from the RGBD images by the visual encoder, the poses of the observed interactive objects in the 3-D space, the categories of all interactive objects, and the indexes of all available actions. The output of the pose estimation module is the next pose $\mathbf { p } _ { t + 1 } ^ { a }$ of the agent for each available action. The pose estimation module predicts the outcomes of each available action for the agent. These predictions are used by the downstream attention and memory module to create compact, action-conditioned representations, and to associate the visual representations with each action.

The visual encoder is fed with an egocentric RGB image captured by a camera and a depth map obtained by a depth sensor

$$
v _ {t} = \mathrm{Cat} \Big (\phi_ {\mathrm{cnn} _ {1}} \big (o _ {t} ^ {\mathrm{RGB}} \big), \phi_ {\mathrm{cnn} _ {2}} \Big (o _ {t} ^ {\mathrm{depth}} \Big) \Big)\tag{1}
$$

where the visual representation v<sub>t</sub> at timestep t is extracted by two respective convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for downstream procedures. The pose estimation module utilizes the segmentation to obtain the pose of each observed object in the 3-D space. During the training stage, the masks of the observed objects are provided by the simulator, while during the validation and testing stage, a pretrained model for object instance segmentation MaskRCNN [61] is applied to extract the masks for the subsequent proceedings, as shown in Fig. 4. Furthermore, one point nearest to the agent is extracted on the segmentation of each observed object. The nearest point for the observed object is obtained by searching the minimum depth in the segment of the depth map. The primary intuition is to compact the related positions of the objects by encoding the nearest point on the surface of the object. Suppose that the agent is located at the current position in the 3-D environment, which can be denoted by $( x _ { t } , y _ { t } , z _ { t } )$ in the coordinate frame. The internal parameters of the depth sensor can be compactly written as a matrix

$$
K = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} f _ {x} & 0 & c _ {x} \\ 0 & f _ {y} & c _ {y} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right]\tag{2}
$$

where $[ f _ { x } ,   f _ { y } ] ^ { T }$ denotes the focal length and $[ c _ { x } , c _ { y } ] ^ { T }$ denotes the optical center. Interactive objects are scattered on the path to the target position. As shown in Fig. 5, the nearest point of each object is backprojected into the 3-D space by using the internal parameters of the depth sensor

$$
\left[\begin{array}{c}\left[\begin{array}{c}x\\y\\1\end{array}\right]\rightarrow \left[\begin{array}{c}X\\Y\\Z\end{array}\right] = F ^ {- 1} = \left[\begin{array}{c}\frac {d (x - c _ {x})}{f _ {x}}\\\frac {d (y - c _ {y})}{f _ {y}}\\d\end{array}\right]\end{array}\right|\tag{3}
$$

where $[ x , y , 1 ] ^ { T }$ denotes the coordinates of a point p on the normalized depth map, $[ X , Y , Z ] ^ { T }$ denotes the coordinates of the corresponding point P in the 3-D space after being backprojecting through the depth sensor, and d denotes the value of depth. We assume that the internal parameters are fixed and will not change during usage. We obtain the internal parameters of the depth sensor from the simulator. Accordingly, the relative poses of the objects are implicit in the coordinates of the nearest points $( X _ { i } , Y _ { i } , Z _ { i } )$ , where i denotes the index of the object. The coordinates are further embedded into hidden features. Meanwhile, the object categories and the action indexes are also embedded into hidden features. We concatenate these three kinds of hidden features with the visual representation v, as shown in Fig. 3. Moreover, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) is utilized to predict the next pose of the agent for each action $a \in { \mathcal { A } } .$ The primary intuition is that the concatenated embeddings contain the information associated with the semantic meaning and the geometric meaning of the current situation of the agent. Hence, the next agent pose implicitly encodes the latent information about the deployed environment and the action-dependent information.

The pose estimation module is trained as a regression problem by predicting the next pose of the agent. The ground-truth pose matrix of the agent can be obtained from the simulator. The L1 loss is utilized to optimize the parameters corresponding to the pose estimation module

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm{PE}} = L 1 \big (\mathbf {p r e d \_ p} _ {t + 1} ^ {a ^ {*}}, \mathbf {g t \_ p} _ {t + 1} ^ {a ^ {*}}\left. \right)\tag{4}
$$

where gt $\mathbf { . p } _ { t + 1 } ^ { a ^ { * } }$ denotes the ground-truth pose of the agent after executing an action $a ^ { * } \in \mathcal { A }$ at timestep $t + 1$ and pred $\mathbf { . p } _ { t + 1 } ^ { a ^ { * } }$ denotes the action-conditioned pose matrix predicted by the pose estimation module. The agent executes only one action $a ^ { * }$ at the timestep t. Hence, we do not backpropagate the gradients of the action indexes that are not executed. We can only collect the ground truth of the next pose matrix for the executed action $a ^ { * }$ and compute the L1 loss. As a result, the gradients are backpropagated only through the path corresponding to the executed action $a ^ { * }$

## D. Attention and Memory Module

As shown in Fig. 3, the architecture of the attention and memory module is a combination of a self-attention layer to summarize discrete embeddings and a GRU state encoder to reason over time. The self-attention layer is utilized to summarize the concatenation of task-related embeddings and the encoded hidden features of the next agent pose into action-conditioned state representations with semantic and geometric information. With the self-attention layer, we enable the agent to have three capabilities: 1) reference the implicit features extracted in the previous steps; 2) make the action-conditioned representations more compact; and 3) directly associate the learned representation to each action.

In addition to extracting the features of the deployed environment, we would like the agent to have implicit representations of its experiences during the exploration in the previous steps. To this end, the memory $h _ { t - 1 }$ of the agent’s history is processed by a GRU state encoder at every timestep t. The output of the self-attention layer and the discrete embeddings (e.g., the visual features v, the poses of observed objects, the categories of all objects, and the indexes of all actions) are concatenated as the global representation. The GRU state encoder takes the global representation as input and exploits the hidden states passed by the previous steps to handle the timing information. The policy network is trained based on the actor–critic framework [62]. After the GRU state encoder, two linear layers are utilized as the actor (to predict probability distributions) and the critic (to produce value estimates). The agent samples an action a to execute in the environment from the action distribution over the action space A. The entire model is trained by a proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm with generalized advantage estimation [63] using fixed-length trajectory segments. In addition, hyperparameter $\alpha \geq 0$ is used to balance the learning of the RL module and the learning of the pose estimation module. The entire learning

## E. State Value Boost Module

For the state-of-the-art on-policy RL method PPO [64] used in the RL setting of this work, the agent learns a discrete control policy $\pi _ { \theta } ( a | s )$ and a state value estimator $V _ { \phi } ( s _ { t } )$ The policy gradients are formed using an action-advantage estimator

$$
\hat {A} = \hat {A} ^ {\pi} (s _ {t}, a _ {t}) = Q ^ {\pi} (a _ {t}, s _ {t}) - V _ {\phi} ^ {\pi} (s _ {t})\tag{6}
$$

where $Q ^ { \pi } ( a _ { t } , s _ { t } )$ denotes the expected return of executing $a _ { t }$ to the environment at state $s _ { t }$ by following policy π. Recent experiences are collected under old policy $\pi _ { \theta _ { \mathrm { o l d } } }$ . More specifically, a truncated version of generalized advantage estimator Â [63] that does not look beyond timestep T is used in this work

$$
\hat {A} _ {t} = \delta_ {t} + (\gamma \lambda) \delta_ {t + 1} + \dots + \dots + (\gamma \lambda) ^ {T - t + 1} \delta_ {T - 1}\tag{7}
$$

where t specifies the timestep in [0, T ], $\gamma \lambda$ denotes a steeper discount, $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ , and $\delta _ { t }$ is formulated as

$$
\delta_ {t} = r _ {t} + \gamma V _ {\phi} (s _ {t + 1}) - V _ {\phi} (s _ {t}).\tag{8}
$$

For minibatches of the recent experience, PPO learns the policy by maximizing a clipped-ratio loss

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\pi} (\theta) = \mathbb {E} _ {t} \big [ \min \big (\rho_ {t} (\theta) \hat {A} _ {t}, \mathrm{clip} (\rho_ {t} (\theta), 1 - \epsilon , 1 + \epsilon) \hat {A} _ {t} \big) \big ]\tag{9}
$$

where $\rho _ { t } ( \theta )$ ρ (θ ) denotes the probability ratio

$$
\rho_ {t} (\theta) = \frac {\pi_ {\theta} (a _ {t} \mid s _ {t})}{\pi_ {\theta_ {\mathrm{old}}} (a _ {t} \mid s _ {t})}\tag{10}
$$

$\pi _ { \theta _ { \mathrm { o l d } } }$ denotes the old policy used for collecting trajectories with parameters $\theta _ { \mathrm { o l d } } ,$ and ϵ is a hyperparameter to clip the probability ratio by moving $\rho _ { t } ( \theta )$ outside of the interval $[ 1 - \epsilon , 1 + \epsilon ]$ . The state value estimator $V _ { \phi } ( s _ { t } )$ is learned as a regression problem with generalized advantage estimation [63]

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {V} (\phi) = \mathbb {E} _ {t} \Big [ \left(V _ {\phi} (s _ {t}) - V _ {t} ^ {\mathrm{targ}}\right) ^ {2} \Big ]\tag{11}
$$

where $V _ { t } ^ { \tt t a r g }$ denotes the target of discounted returns.

The state value boost module focuses on the data-efficient regime to optimize the performance by processing the image observations with stochastic augmentations. Crucially, in the IVN tasks, the high-dimensional image-based observations are indirect representation of the state: $o _ { t } = O ( s _ { t } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ . In this work, either random crop or motion blur can be applied to image observations during the training stage. The augmented image observations $f _ { \mathrm { a u g } } ( o _ { t } )$ are embedded into visual features $v _ { t }$ by the visual encoder. At each timestep, image augmentations allow the generalization of several surrogate observations with the same state values. M state samples ${ s _ { t } } ^ { * } \sim \mu ( \cdot )$ are generated via image augmentations for an arbitrary distribution of states $\mu ( \cdot )$ . Hence, the variance of the state value estimator $V _ { \phi } ( s _ { t } )$ can be reduced in this mechanism. More specifically, the state value estimate can be obtained from

$$
\left| \underset {s \sim \mu (\cdot)} {\mathbb {E}} \left[ V _ {\phi} (s _ {t}) \right] \approx \frac {1}{M} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} V _ {\phi} \left(s _ {t} ^ {*}\right) \right|.\tag{12}
$$

The details of the state value boost module are given as Algorithm 1.

## IV. EXPERIMENTS

In this section, the details of the IVN tasks, the implementation, and the comparative baselines are introduced first. Then, the evaluation metrics and the quantitative results are described. Moreover, the ablation studies are elaborated, and the training metrics are visualized followed by the case study.

## A. Settings

1) Task Details: The IVN task in this article is to navigate an embodied agent from a random starting point to a random goal point. The path to the goal point is blocked by interactive objects on the floor. Hence, the agent should learn to move the obstacles out of the way to reach the destination and invoke the action $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ to indicate the completion of the task. The IVN tasks pose a set of challenges, including fore active perception, long-horizon planning, and reasoning about the next pose of the agent caused by the possible action.

2) Environment Settings: We demonstrate the performance of the proposed PTRL framework using a high-fidelity simulator AI2-iTHOR [46], which is built on Unity game engine and is extensible to accommodate new types of interactive objects. Meanwhile, the baselines are reimplemented in AI2-iTHOR. Twenty interactive objects are used to conduct the experiments: ArmChair, DogBed, Box, Chair, Desk, DiningTable, SideTable, Sofa, Stool, Television, Pillow, Bread, Apple, AlarmClock, Lettuce, GarbageCan, Laptop, Microwave, Pot, and Tomato. The agent can interact with the environment by applying force to individual objects. A camera and a depth sensor are mounted on the agent. Egocentric $2 2 4   \times   2 2 4   \times   3$ RGB images and $2 2 4   \times   2 2 4   \times   1$ depth images are captured from the agent’s current viewpoint $( 9 0 ^ { \circ } ~ \mathrm { F O V } )$ . The current relative coordinates to the goal point are given by the environment. Predefining the action space in an uncertain and interactive environment is an iterative and dynamic process that constantly refines the capabilities of an agent to effectively address environmental challenges and task requirements. In defining the action space for IVN tasks, we adopt the approach of prior works and establish the action space for our agent as $\mathcal { A } = \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { M o v e A h e a d } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { R o t a t e R i g h t } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { R o t a t e L e f t } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { L o o k D o u n } } \cup$ $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { L o o k U p } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { P u s h } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { P u l l } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { R i g h t P u s h } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { L e f t P u s h } } \cup \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { E N D } } .$ $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { M o v e A h e a d } }$ results in the agent moving ahead by 0.25 m unless the action would result in a collision. A<sub>RotateRight</sub> results in the agent changing the azimuth angle by $9 0 ^ { \circ }$ , and $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { R o t a t e L e f t } }$ changes the azimuth angle by $- 9 0 ^ { \circ } . ~ \mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { { L } } }$ <sub>ookDown</sub> results in the agent lowering its camera angle by 3090◦, and $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { L o o k U p } }$ raises the camera angle by 3090◦. The action $a \in \{ \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { P u s h } } , \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { P u l l } } , \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { R i g h t P u s h } } , \mathcal { A } _ { \mathtt { L e f t P u s h } } \}$ results in the agent applying a force of 100 N to move the closest observed object in a specified direction. $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ results in the episode immediately terminating. The dimensions of this action space enable the agent to engage in a variety of actions, such as moving, changing viewing angles, and applying force to objects.

3) Datasets: The experiments are conducted on the obstacle navigation datasets introduced in [27]. There are 120 scenes of four room categories: Living Rooms, Bedrooms, and Bathrooms and Kitchens. Fig. 6 shows the top-down perspective for one instance of each room category. For each room category, 20 scenes are used for training, five scenes are used for validation, and five scenes are used for testing. The interactive objects are randomly placed as obstacles to block the path to the goal point. For the interactive objects, the simulator provides five variations of 20 categories. Four variations of each object category are randomly selected for training. The last variation of each object is used for testing.

## B. Implementation Details

1) Model Architecture: It is challenging to simultaneously train the visual encoder and the RL networks using RL meth ods. In this work, the entire model is trained by a reward-based method PPO [64] using the loss function $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { R L } }$ in RL, and the visual encoder can also be updated by loss function $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { P E } }$ in supervised representation learning. The hyperparameter α used to balance $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { R L } }$ and $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { R E } }$ is set to 3. During the training stage, we update the model every 30 steps with Adam optimizer. The initial learning rate is set to $3   \times   1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ and linearly decays to 0. All model parameters are trained end-to-end for 10 million steps simultaneously with 80 processes of 80 different scenes in the training datasets. The discounting parameter γ in RL training is set to 0.99, the parameter of generalized advantage estimator $\lambda _ { \mathrm { g a e } }$ is set to 0.95, and the clipped gradients $\Delta$ satisfy with $| \Delta | \; < = 0 . 5 .$ The features of RGB image and depth image are extracted by the visual encoder using two CNNs and fused by a linear layer. During the training stage, the ground-truth object masks are provided by the simulator. A pretrained MaskRCNN [61] (ResNet-50 [4], trained on the training scenes) is employed to extract the segmentation of the RGB image during the testing stage. For the MaskRCNN, we set the object prediction score to 0.5, the segmentation probability to 0.1, and the output classes to 21. The output classes include a background class and 20 interactive object classes. The key, query, and value are embedded by three MLPs in the self-attention layer. A linear layer for the policy (actor) and a linear layer for the value (critic) are followed by a GRU state encoder. In the state value boost module, we set the number of image augmentations $M = 2$ to regularize the value function as described in Section III-E.

2) Reward Settings: Our hypothesis is that the long-horizon planning ability can be learned through the reward signal received by the agent. In this work, the reward function is proposed as follows:

$$
R = R _ {\mathrm{suc}} + R _ {\mathrm{pot}} + R _ {\mathrm{int}} + R _ {\mathrm{step}}.\tag{13}
$$

$R _ { \mathrm { s u c } }$ (short for success reward) denotes a one-time sparse reward and is set to 10 only when the agent converges to the goal point and invokes the action $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ $R _ { \mathrm { p o t } }$ (short for potential reward) denotes the difference in geodesic distance [31] (the shortest path distance in the environment) between the goal point and the agent in the current and previous steps. $R_{\mathrm{pot}} = \mathrm{GD}_{t-1} - \mathrm{GD}_{t}$ , where $\mathbf { G } \mathbf { D } _ { t }$ denotes the geodesic distance at timestep $t . ~ R _ { \mathrm { p o t } }$ is set to positive when the geodesic distance decreases and negative when the geodesic distance increases. $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ is set to encourage the agent to learn to open a path by interacting with the obstacles. When the action resulted in blocking the path from the agent to the goal, $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } } = - 0 . 5 .$ . If a path was opened by the agent’s action, $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } } = 0 . 5 . ~ R _ { \mathrm { s t e p } }$ is set as a time consumption penalty to −0.01 at each timestep.

3) Sample Efficiency Analysis: The reward function is engineered to train the agent’s behavior toward efficient navigation while facilitating interaction with objects within densely cluttered environments. Sample efficiency is a metric that quantifies the number of samples required by a learning agent to reach a performance threshold [65]. However, in navigation tasks based on image inputs, the reward signals are sparse and the sample efficiency of RL is considerably low [25]. Fig. 7 shows how the modules of the PTRL framework enhance sample efficiency during the training stage. The pose estimation module and the attention and memory module are designed to provide supervisory signals for representation learning, thereby improving the learning efficiency of RL. This aligns with prior research [66] demonstrating that learning auxiliary tasks can effectively enhance both the performance and sample efficiency of RL. Furthermore, the state value boost module is specifically designed to enhance sample efficiency by mitigating overfitting during training. This concept resonates with the methodology proposed in previous work [41] on data-regularized policies.

## C. Baselines

The proposed PTRL framework is compared with the following baseline methods with the same learning hyperparameters in a visual encoder and policy network. The visual encoder and policy network are trained by PPO [64]. The proposed modules in PTRL and modular training dramatically improve PPO’s performance.

1) PPO: It denotes the agent [64] trained with PPO, and the visual inputs are an RGB image with a depth map. PPO is a widely used deep RL algorithm and simultaneously trains a visual encoder network alongside a navigation control policy network [31].

2) PBL: It denotes a PPO-based method with predictions of bootstrapped latents to enhance self-supervised representation learning for deep RL [67].

3) NIE: It denotes a method that jointly plans a series of actions and explicitly predicts the effect of those actions in the scene [27].

## D. Evaluation Metrics

To quantify the performance of the proposed PTRL framework while remaining reasonably interpretable and straightforward, we follow the prior works [27], [31], [56] and use the evaluation metrics as follows.

The first measure is success rate (SR). SR denotes the ratio of the number of episodes where the agent was successful to the total number of episodes. The action $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ indicates that the agent understands the goal point that has been reached and has concluded the navigation episode. Thus, a navigation episode is deemed successful only if the agent is sufficiently close to the goal point and invokes the action $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ . Specifically, the threshold for reaching the goal point is set to 0.2 m in the experiments.

The second measure is average final geodesic distance (AFGD), between the agent to the goal point. Rather than using Euclidean distance, using geodesic distance takes the geometric structure of the scenario into account. The episode ends when it reaches the maximum allowed steps or the agent invokes the action $\mathcal { A } _ { \mathrm { E N D } }$ . The maximum number of allowed steps for the agent is set to 500 in the experiments.

The third measure is success weighted by (normalized inverse) path length (SPL), which is introduced in [31] recently for the evaluation of pure navigation agents. SPL is a summary measure of the performance as follows:

$$
\left| \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} S _ {i} \frac {\ell_ {i}}{\max \left(p _ {i} , \ell_ {i}\right)} \right|\tag{14}
$$

where N denotes the total number of episodes, $S _ { i }$ is the binary indicator of success in episode i, $\ell _ { i }$ denotes the geodesic distance from the starting point to the goal point in episode i , and $p _ { i }$ denotes the path length of the agent in episode i. It should be underscored that the SPL metric is stringent, as it computes the geodesic path while neglecting the obstacles present in the environment. The agents are subjected to testing in environments of significant complexity which they have not previously encountered. Hence, we suggest that a joint consideration of both SR and SPL metrics might yield a more robust evaluation of performance, as they highlight distinct elements of competency.

## E. Qualitative Results

The effectiveness of the proposed PTRL framework and the baselines are evaluated in the virtual simulator AI2-iTHOR. During the testing stage, the categories of the scenes are Living Rooms, Bedrooms, Bathrooms, and Kitchens, same as the categories during the training stage. For each category during the testing stage, there are five previously unseen scenes. The 2500 IVN tasks are conducted for evaluation. In each task, the shortest path from the starting point to the goal point is blocked by previously unseen variations of the interactive objects.

Deep RL is well known for the instability of results across different random seeds as well as machines. Hence, the experiments are implemented for the purposes of fair comparisons with the following two simple rules. First, the results of the frameworks are obtained by training and evaluating with three different random seeds. The final qualitative numbers are the average of the results achieved by each framework. Second, we reimplement the baselines, retrain the models by different random seeds, and compare the averaging performance against the results in previous papers. If the authors of prior works made their pretrained models public, we also take the results of the pretrained models into account. The training process was performed using two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs, running for approximately 70 h. The best numbers of each baseline and the results of the proposed PTRL framework are shown in Table II. The symbols ↑ and ↓ are used to show whether larger or smaller values are better.

During the testing stage, the PTRL framework significantly outperforms the existing methods, especially improving the SPL score from 31.3% to 34.4%. The improvement can also be consistently observed that the SR is increased from 80.0% to 82.4% and the AVGD is decreased from 0.304 to 0.276 m. PTRL is more generalized to previously unseen scenarios compared with the baselines. In summary, the results justify the effectiveness of using the proposed model, and PTRL outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines in all the measures.

## F. Visualizing the Training Metrics

Note that the performance during the testing stage is more important than the performance during the training stage. We still report three important metrics of the baseline algorithms during the training process. Right actions at every timestep led to better results in the IVN tasks than wrong actions. Hence, the complementary curves provide more signals to the change in navigation performance during the training stage. It can be seen from Fig. 8(a) that PTRL significantly outperforms the baselines in SPL score. We believe that the agent can successfully learn to interact with the obstacles and further improve its efficiency. As shown in Fig. 8(b), the average geodesic distance to the goal point decreases, and the agent can complete the tasks in most cases from the perspective of the tasks to arrive at the goal point. As shown in Fig. 8(c), the episode length increases when the training starts because the agent begins to explore the environment and try to arrive at the goal point. Guided by the reward function, the agent tries to find the shortest path as the episode length begins to decrease at about 5 million training steps. To some extent, we believe that the change in the episode length shows that the agent gets a better understanding of the environment and the IVN tasks during the training process.

## G. Self-Supervised Learning for Representation

The proposed PTRL framework explicitly predicts the next pose of the agent conditioned on the actions to bootstrap the learning process of the visual encoder. The self-supervised learning (SSL) objective makes the downstream RL training process more stable. Furthermore, SSL can be applied at various stages in the process of IVN tasks based on visual input. We further compare our proposed framework PTRL with three different state-of-the-art SSL methods. Specifically, CRL [68] leverages the SimCLR objective to pretrain the visual encoder, utilizing an image dataset collected by the agent in an online setting. IMAIL [69] jointly trains the visual encoder and downstream networks, utilizing an SSL optimization objective, specifically image reconstruction. BSE [10] employs SSL, predicting the subsequent waypoint, to enhance the learning efficiency of both the state and visual encoders. The overall results are markedly sensitive to initialization. For a fair comparison, we reimplement the SSL component of the methods to operate on multiple GPUs and establish the training phases to 10 million steps within AI2-iTHOR scenes. Qualitative results, averaged over three random seeds, are shown in Table III. The findings emphasize the advantageous role of SSL for enhancing generalization in IVN tasks. It is evident that the utilization of auxiliary objectives during training can bolster performance on IVN tasks. Furthermore, the performance of the PTRL framework, with its focus on predicting task-related latents, outperforms current state-of-the-art methodologies.

## H. Ablation Studies

For ablation studies, we further evaluate the variations of the proposed framework as follows. The quantitative results are shown in Table IV. The **End-to-end** model represents a benchmark for IVN tasks in interactive environments, where agents formulate decisions exclusively based on their current partial observations, without integrating historical information into their decision-making [56]. The **PE only** model signifies an approach where the pose estimation module aids in training the end-to-end RL navigation networks. This model leverages pose estimation as a means to provide supplementary guidance and enhance the performance. The **SVB only** model is implemented to understand whether the state value boost module can help RL incorporate image augmentations into input observations and improve transfer to previously unseen scenarios. The state value boost module undergoes image augmentation via random cropping, wherein the original image is displaced by an extent of 8 pixels. The primary intuition is to imbue the value networks with additional translation invariance. We first pad each side of egocentric RGBD images with 8 pixels. The value of the extended pixel is repeated the same as the boundary pixels. Specifically, an original $2 2 4   \times   2 2 4$ pixel image could be extended to a $2 4 0   \times   2 4 0$ pixel image. Then, a random patch of $2 2 4   \times   2 2 4$ pixels is selected as the image input to the state value boost module, as shown in Fig. 9(b). Each time RGBD images are sampled from the reply buffer during the training, this procedure is repeated. We reimplement the model with the number of state value augmentations $M   =   2$ and keep all the hyperparameters the same as the end-to-end baseline. We noticed that in [70] that the improvements provided by the image augmentation strategies are still not sufficient enough to redeem lost performance. However, as shown in Table IV, the state value boost module improves the performance during the unseen test stage, compared with the end-to-end baseline. We believe that in complex IVN tasks with more actions, the state value boost module reduces overfitting greatly by closing the performance gap of the visual encoder between the similar observations. We extend our tests to ascertain whether another form of input perturbation, specifically motion blur, can be employed to regularize the value function in the state value boost module, as shown in Fig. 9(c). The key intuition is to equip the value networks with additional resistance to motion blur, a common artifact arising from the robot’s jittery movements. Our results yield similar performance metrics, suggesting that a straightforward image augmentation strategy effectively enhances the performance of the fundamental RL networks. We applied the proposed state value boost module in the iGibson Challenge 2021 and won second place in the interactive navigation track. The **PE & AM** model is implemented by incorporating the integration of two distinct modules: the pose estimation module and the attention and memory module. The latter module implicitly associates the learned representation with each corresponding action, utilizing historical information collected throughout task execution and encoding these data as the current state in the downstream RL policy networks. Notably, the inclusion of the attention and memory module results in significant performance enhancements. The **PE & SVB** model is implemented through the integration of both the pose estimation module and the state value boost module. Results from this dual-module integration underscore not only the benefits derived from their conjunction but also illuminate the considerable contribution of the attention and memory module to the proposed full PTRL model. The synergistic employment of these components markedly augments the model’s performance, bolstering the effectiveness of our proposed framework. The **PTRL** $\mathbf { w } / \mathbf { 1 }   \times   \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { P E } }$ model is implemented to provide an in-depth analysis of the proposed modules’ contributions. The parameter α is strategically adjusted to maintain an equilibrium between $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { P E } }$ and $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { R L } }$ throughout the model’s comprehensive training process. In this particular implementation, α is reduced to 1, thereby elucidating the impact of $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { P E } }$ . This analysis furnishes insights into the potential adverse effects that a low value of parameter α could impose on the final outcome. Alternatively, in the **PTRL** $\mathbf { w / 1 0 } \times \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { P E } }$ model, we augment the value of parameter α to 10, offering a perspective on the repercussions of a larger value of parameter α on the final result.

## I. Case Study

Five positive examples in the IVN tasks are shown in Fig. 10. Each row indicates a successful episode that the agent learns to interact with the obstacles to reach the goal point in different room types. We can observe from Fig. 10 that: 1) the agent can dynamically adjust its pose and choose right actions according to its distance to the objects on the path to the goal point as well as the structure of the local environment, which satisfies the expectation that the agent can learn to unblock the path by interacting with the objects to adapt to the complex condition and perform the IVN tasks, and 2) the learned policy significantly generalizes to different previously unseen scenarios and the series of executed actions can handle multiple obstacles with long-horizon planning.

We further showcase two kinds of common errors in Fig. 11. The top row shows that the goal point was finally covered by the Television because the agent failed to push the Television in the right direction. The episode was quitted by the agent to avoid an unreasonable long trajectory. The bottom row shows an example that the path to the goal was blocked by a huge ${ \cal S } o f a .$ . The episode ended with a hopeless trajectory. During the training stage, these corner cases were not well trained, so the agent failed to solve these problems. The two negative examples suffer from the error accumulation issues, where the subsequence of wrong actions are caused by one wrong decision at the beginning [71]. It is evident that the proposed PTRL framework still faces challenges in the context of IVN tasks. The primary challenge lies in managing the episodic memory arising from the partial observations of the egocentric visual agent. The agent might still potentially encounter dilemmas when deployed in an unfamiliar environment. Hence, learning to foresee and recover from errors is desired for further study. Moreover, while RNNs are traditionally utilized to aggregate past observations and actions, thereby endowing the agent’s policy with memory, their capacity to capture long-term spatiotemporal information is limited. The state space continues to be expansive, posing substantial challenges for exploration. In recent research, attention mechanisms have emerged as a promising alternative to RNNs, enhancing the integration of visual and geometric data from historical exploration [6], [10]. Looking ahead, our future research will delve deeper into the strategy of image tokenization [72] to effectively reduce the dimensionality of the state space into the latent space. Leveraging attention mechanisms, we anticipate being able to further process long-term historical information into episodic memory.

## V. CONCLUSION

In this article, we present a novel PTRL framework, which combines supervised representation learning, self-attention mechanism, and data augmentation in the context of the IVN tasks. In the PTRL framework, we incorporate the pose estimation module, which focuses on facilitating representation learning for the downstream navigation control policy. We utilize an attention and memory module to associate the visual representation to each action and exploit spatiotemporal dependencies. Furthermore, data augmentation is employed to leverage input perturbations and regularize the value function. Extensive results of evaluations illustrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework in increasing accuracy. The proposed framework shows a better generalization capacity in unseen environments. We believe that the idea of facilitating representation learning for downstream RL policy with task-related predictions is commonly applicable to navigation tasks. Moreover, the proposed modular framework allows the components to be optimized separately, and each module can be generally adapted to other navigation tasks.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Liang Yuan** (Member, IEEE) received the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in electrical and computer engineering from The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA, in 2010 and 2011, respectively.

He is currently a Professor with the College of Information Science and Technology and the Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Soft Matter Science and Engineering, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing, China. He was honored with the National Recruitment Program of Global Experts in 2014. His research interests include computer

vision and imaging processes, robotics, and automation in life science.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Yue Lu** (Senior Member, IEEE) received the B.S. degree in wireless technology and the M.S. degree in telecommunications and electronic systems from Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China, in 1990 and 1993, respectively, and the Ph.D. degree in pattern recognition and intelligent systems from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China, in 2000.

He is currently a Professor and the Dean of the School of Communication and Electronic Engineering, East China Normal University, Shanghai. Prior to joining East China Normal University in 2004,

he was a Research Fellow with the Department of Computer Science, National University of Singapore, Singapore. He has contributed to more than 150 peer-reviewed publications in journals and conferences. He holds 19 authorized patents. His research interests include pattern recognition and machine learning, image processing and machine vision, machine intelligence, and intelligent systems.

Dr. Lu is serving as an Associate Editor for the Pattern Recognition journal.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Jiwei Shen is currently pursuing the Ph.D. degree with the Shanghai Key Laboratory of Multidimensional Information Processing, School of Communication and Electronic Engineering, East China Normal University, Shanghai, China, supervised by Prof. Yue Lu.

His research interests include reinforcement learning, computer vision, robotics, lithography processes, and automation in semiconductor manufacturing.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Shujing Lyu** received the Ph.D. degree in computer application technology from East China Normal University, Shanghai, China, in 2014.

She is currently a Research Professor with the School of Communication and Electronic Engineering, East China Normal University. Her research interests include character recognition, text and image processing, computer vision, and machine learning.
